SCENE CONTEXT
The Lamp — a grotty backstreet South-East London pub, late night, autumn 2011. Three broke mates are slumped around the little corner table after a gig that paid them nothing. The skinny one, Oli, suddenly lights up with a drunken idea — to go and nick the red boat. Deflated turning manic, boozy and feverish. One single continuous handheld shot, 5 seconds.

Foreground: the small round cast-iron pedestal table with pints and a full ashtray, lit by the warm cream-shaded pendant directly above it. Behind the banquette: the deep-green wall with the faded painted cosmos mural and two small framed black-and-white photos. Screen-left: the open maroon four-panel door under the "GENTS" sign, white tiles and punk band posters inside. FIRST FRAME AND SPATIAL BLOCKING
The first visible frame already contains all three men at the table — no empty establishing frame, no delayed reveal. HORACE on the banquette screen-left, back to the green wall under the cosmos mural, torso three-quarter to camera, head down. CAL on the banquette screen-right beside him, hunched over his pint. OLI on a wooden stool on the near side of the table, screen-right foreground, turned three-quarter back toward the other two. The warm pendant pools light on the table between them. Readable immediately as three beaten, drunk mates.

FORMAT MODE
Single continuous take, 5 seconds. The camera does not cut by itself. Real-time motion.

OPTICS
47° diagonal field of view, standard normal lens character, natural human-eye perspective, camera physically close at the table. Comfortable depth of field, the booth and the surrounding pub (GENTS door, window, bar) readable around the men, faces natural and undistorted. Framing tightens only because the camera physically pushes in — the lens does not change. No lens drift.

CAMERA
Low handheld rig at table-top height, slight three-quarter angle from the open front-right of the booth. Operator breath, micro-settling, human weight corrections — no digital jitter. A slow, steady push-in across the 5 seconds, easing from a loose three-shot to a loose single favouring OLI. Focus holds on the table group, then settles on OLI's face at the payoff.

ACTION TIMING
0.0s to 1.5s — the three slumped and beaten: CAL stares into his pint, HORACE exhales and drags a hand down his face, OLI stares at nothing, jiggling his knee. Drunken, flat.
1.5s to 3.0s — OLI's eyes snap wide as the idea lands; he jolts forward off his slump and leans hard over the little table toward the other two, jabbing a finger at them.
3.0s to 5.0s — OLI grins and lays out the plan with both hands; CAL lifts his head, HORACE turns toward OLI with a wary look. The camera settles into a loose single on OLI's lit-up face. Hold.

PHYSICS
When OLI lurches forward the small pedestal table rocks; the pints slop against the glass and a little beer rings the table. Cigarette smoke drifts and re-layers under the pendant. HORACE's afro carries a slight bounce on his head-turn. Clothing and hair move with natural delay; the men's weight settles into the leather banquette and the stool.

Low pub ambience — a muffled jukebox, a faint fruit-machine jingle, clinking glasses, a couple of old regulars murmuring offscreen. Grounded naturalistic photoreal cinema, late-September 2011 SE London, no modern tech. ARRI Alexa, vintage spherical primes, subtle anamorphic, widescreen. Low warm-tungsten grade against deep green, blacks rich but not crushed. Clean and sharp, no grain, no overexposure.

— SEGMENT 1 — 0.0s to 2.5s — WIDE ESTABLISHING (LOCATION TEST) —
FIRST FRAME: the full room exactly as image1, all three men already seated together on the curved banquette behind the round table — CAL left, HORAS centre, OLI right — empty pint glasses on the table, the pub softly hazy. The location reads immediately and fills the frame.
OPTICS: 28mm vintage spherical prime, wide establishing, camera set back across the room — straight architectural lines stay rectilinear, no fisheye; the seated men sit at mid-distance and read at honest human scale.
CAMERA: low eye-level wide, static, faint handheld breath only — no push, no drift. Matches the image1 composition.
ACTION: the waiter steps in from screen-right and sets a fresh pint down on the round table among the empties, then steps back toward the bar; the lads barely stir.
PHYSICS: the waiter walks with real weight; the fresh pint's head sloshes and settles with a soft ring against the empties; ambient haze drifts as he passes.
HARD CUT at 2.5s.

— SEGMENT 2 — 2.5s to 4.0s — CLOSE-UP, HORAS —
FIRST FRAME: tight close-up on HORAS, sharp, framed from the centre of the booth; behind him the green wall with framed photos and pendant glow in soft smoky bokeh. A cigarette is between his lips, unlit. CAL's spot stays to screen-left, OLI's to screen-right (kept consistent with the wide).
OPTICS: 80mm vintage spherical prime, close portrait — HORAS razor-sharp, shallow depth of field, background compressed and soft.
CAMERA: low, near eye level, static, faint handheld breath. Focus on HORAS.
ACTION: HORAS flicks a lighter, the flame catches, he lights the cigarette and takes the first draw; smoke curls past his face. He turns his eyes screen-right toward OLI and asks, dry and weary.
DIALOGUE (HORAS, British/Essex accent): "Is this slop?" Only HORAS speaks; his gaze is on OLI off-frame screen-right.
PHYSICS: lighter flame flickers with his breath; the tip embers brighter on the draw; a real plume of smoke rises and drifts; afro and tee settle naturally.
HARD CUT at 4.0s.

— SEGMENT 3 — 4.0s to 6.0s — CLOSE-UP, OLI —
FIRST FRAME: tight close-up on OLI, sharp, reclined on the RIGHT of the booth; behind him the dark-wood bar, brass beer pumps and the Union Jack in soft smoky bokeh. The fresh pint is in his hand. HORAS's spot stays to screen-left (consistent positions).
OPTICS: 80mm vintage spherical prime, close portrait — OLI razor-sharp, shallow depth of field, background soft and compressed.
CAMERA: low, near eye level, static, faint handheld breath. Focus on OLI.
ACTION: OLI lifts the pint, takes a slow sip, lets it settle, glances screen-left toward HORAS and answers heavily.
DIALOGUE (OLI, British/Essex accent): "I wish I knew, mate." Only OLI speaks.
PHYSICS: the beer tilts and settles in the glass; his weight stays slumped into the leather banquette; smoke haze drifts past in the air.

All movement has weight and contact; clothing and the big afro move with natural delay; a constant soft ambient haze drifts through every frame. Only HORAS's lit cigarette produces actual smoke; in the wide (Segment 1) no one is smoking and no smoke comes from anyone's mouth.

LIGHTING
Warm tungsten practicals from image1 (pendant lamps, wall sconce, brass-pump glints) as the key, diffused and softened by the haze so faces stay gently lit and readable, never flat. Deep green walls and oxblood dado sit in low shadow; cool counter-notes from the GENTS doorway and the bar window. No flat front light.

HORAS lights a cigarette and says only "Is this slop?"; OLI sips and says only "I wish I knew, mate" — both in a British/Essex accent, no other dialogue, no subtitles. Keep honest human scale, no one oversized or shrunken. Soft ambient haze throughout; only HORAS's cigarette smokes. Period-accurate 2011, no modern tech. Photoreal, stable picture, sharp clarity.

No empty establishing frame, no delayed reveal.

CAMERA
Eye level, inside the cabin, behind and beside the officer. Aggressive raw handheld — strong operator shake, jolts, weight shifts, hard micro-corrections — as if braced in a vibrating airframe. The whole frame also rolls and dips as the helicopter banks: the horizon and city lights outside the door tilt to the left through the shot. Camera fights to keep Quinn in frame.

ACTION TIMING
0.0s to 4.0s: helicopter banks left; the cabin and the view out the door roll with it. Quinn tightens her grip on the overhead rail, steadies herself against the tilt, and leans slightly out and down toward the ground below, eyes fixed on a single point outside. The officer holds his aim out the door, tracking the same point.

11.0s to 15.0s: Quinn lowers the megaphone a few centimeters but keeps staring down, jaw set, waiting. The bank continues to ease. Ambient rotor noise fills the silence after the line.

The megaphone and rifle carry visible weight; wrists and arms react to it. The kneeling officer's body absorbs the vibration and the roll.

LIGHTING
Dim, motivated only by the cabin's existing sources — the cold cyan-green glow of the cockpit instrument panel and overhead monitor, plus faint city light spilling through the open door. Low-key exposure; faces fall into shadow. Quinn's face is lit only by the weak instrument glow and edge light from the doorway, much of it in deep shadow, cheekbone and brow catching a faint cool rim. No artificial fill, no added key light, no flat frontal light.

AUDIO
Loud continuous rotor and wind roar. Quinn's single megaphone line, electronically amplified and slightly distorted, beginning at 4.0s and finishing by 11.0s. No other dialogue, no narration, no subtitles, no music. After the line, only rotor and wind remain.

POSITIVE LOCKS
Exactly two people in frame: Detective Quinn at the door and the kneeling officer in the foreground. Quinn's gaze stays locked on one fixed point outside and below throughout. The officer's rifle stays aimed on the same line as Quinn's look. One hand stays on the overhead rail. Quinn speaks only the scripted line, once. The helicopter visibly banks left. Scene 10, combined shots 1–2 as one continuous take. Cal slips out of a loud dressing room into the dim graffiti backstage corridor of The Commons, leaves the chaos behind the door, crosses to the wall by the bare bulb, leans against it and dials his daughter from memory. As the call connects he drops into a deliberately gruff fake "policeman" voice, half-turning to hide a smile.

SCENE CONTEXT
阴天冬日的伦敦粗野主义住宅区，湖边一条带连续方形混凝土桥墩的高架步道旁。 中的男人（Dmitry）正在激烈交火：他贴在混凝土墙角与桥墩后躲避，用一把 AK-47 向特种部队还击，同时面无表情地哼唱俄语歌曲《喀秋莎》；偶尔在枪响时或有混凝土碎片擦身飞过时微微眯眼；当他扣动 AK 扳机开火时，他唱得更大声，几乎是在呐喊。受控多镜头，全程硬切，写实，动态枪战。

Cinematic film still, shot on ARRI Alexa with Cooke S4 prime lenses, deep rich filmic tones, fine film grain, 2.39:1 widescreen. A cramped top-floor council bedsit on a deck-access estate in South-East London, foggy mid-morning, late September 2011. Reverse diagonal, wide eye-level shot of two flat straight green-painted walls meeting at one clean right-angle corner deep in the room, the two walls set wide apart with a broad span of open wooden floor between them. The same flat as its matching front shot: muted drowned green-grey painted plaster, a low ceiling crossed by a boxed structural beam with a fringed cloth pinned to it, an exposed yellow-brick pillar, worn wooden floorboards with overlapping faded Persian rugs, cool foggy daylight, no people, empty room.

The right-hand wall is the main wall: an old silver CRT television on a low stand centred flat against it; a small low cupboard right beside the television; on the wall above and beside it, faded grime and hip-hop posters that blend into the room — sun-bleached, desaturated, low-contrast and weathered, never bright or eye-catching — a grime MC portrait and a couple of small gig flyers, plus a small black "CULLY HILL BOYS" spray tag. A low teak coffee table stands out on the floor a short way in front of the television, between the TV and the camera, its long edge parallel to the wall, a mug, a notebook and papers on it — out in the room facing the TV, not beside it and not against the wall.

The left-hand wall, far across the room, is flat and plain with a closed scuffed inner toilet door bearing a hand-written sign that reads "FUCK OFF WHILE I'M PEEIN", a metal bin beside it. Bottom-left of frame, a corner of the faded petrol-teal corduroy sofa just clips into view.

Lit solely by soft cool foggy daylight from an off-frame window with a faint warm spill from an off-frame lamp. Clean neutral colour, no muddy cast, the green only as real wall surface, deep but soft shadows, gentle filmic contrast, true blacks held softly, lived-in but not squalid.

SCENE CONTEXT
Per the director's storyboard: a wide shot — three gunshots crack from somewhere deep in the fog down the channel, and a flock of crows bursts off the boats and scatters into the sky. Violence with no visible culprit. The shooters are never seen.

OPTICS
63° diagonal field of view, wide-normal lens character (≈35mm, per the director's 28–35mm), camera about 1 metre above the channel water with a slight upward tilt, anamorphic widescreen. Wide even view of the channel, boat rows to the edges, straight lines rectilinear, fog hiding the far depth.

CAMERA
Static observational and calm for a beat, then the one kinetic strike of the scene: a hard focus-snap and a startled upward whip-pan following the rising crows; human, jolted, not a smooth move; back toward stillness by the end.

LIGHTING
Cold flat blue-teal fog, the two sodium lamps glowing orange deep down the channel near the hidden gunfire; the crows read as dark shapes against the lighter foggy sky as they rise. Low-key, no added light on the gunfire source, expose for the haze.

ACTIVE REFERENCES

Use it as the source of geography, layout, materials and cold atmosphere for this wide channel shot; the gunfire stays hidden deep in the fog, off-plate. NEVER use the reference as the first/start frame and never reproduce its framing — the shot opens on its own composition. Keep the tag exactly as written.

LOCATION MAP
Built from <<<315a29fb-6585-4329-83bc-fa6794fc1b69>>>. Bray Marina on the Thames at night, pre-dawn fog. A central channel of still black water runs straight into the mist to a vanishing point. Twin rows of moored white cabin cruisers and motor yachts flank screen-left and screen-right, covered, with tall sailboat masts far right. Two sodium lamps glow warm orange in the mid-distance haze — one just left of centre, one just right of centre — each trailing a single vertical orange reflection down the channel water. Right foreground: a round manicured topiary tree on a curved stone embankment. Left foreground: a matching curved stone embankment edge. Reeds and iris stalks and scattered autumn leaves line the banks. Cold blue-teal fog throughout. The gunfire source is hidden deep in the fog near the two sodium lamps, behind the moored boats, never shown.

FIRST FRAME AND SPATIAL BLOCKING
The first frame is this shot's own wide channel composition at water level — never the reference plate used as a still — the quiet channel with crows visibly perched across the foreground and midground boat rails, x 20%–80%, y 40%–65%, the two sodium lamps glowing deep at centre. On the gunshots the birds launch upward together and exit the top of frame. No human figures, no muzzle flash shown — only the reaction.

ACTION TIMING
0.0s to 0.6s: stillness. 0.6s: BANG — first shot, the nearest crows flinch. 0.9s: BANG — second shot, the flock launches. 1.2s: BANG — third shot, the camera jolts and whips up as all birds scatter into the sky by 2.0s.

PHYSICS
Real bird take-off: wings beating hard, bodies accelerating upward with downbeat thrust, staggered launch timing across the flock, air disturbance. No recoil shown on the hidden shooters.

EDITING / TRANSITION
A hard editorial accent lands on EACH of the three gunshots — three sharp punctuation beats — in stark contrast to the surrounding silence.

AUDIO
No music. Three dry, sharp gunshots with hard transient cracks, an explosion of wing beats and crow alarm calls, then air. Grime beat still absent.

(NO "ONE LADLE" sign.)
<<<9cfdf26f-ada4-42e1-b409-551631412bec>>> — late 20s, ~1.75 m, curly black hair under a TEAL hairnet, beard + glasses; cream POLO; dark-TEAL stained BIB apron; blue jeans; olive trainers; serving ladle in hand. 3 views. match 100%.

═══ 2. STYLE ═══
8K IMAX photoreal — no 3D/game look. ARRI Alexa, vintage spherical primes, subtle anamorphic. 180° shutter blur. Pore-level skin, wet living eyes, breath/chest rise. Gravity + contact shadows, no floating props. 24fps, 8K, no jitter. Cinematic 2.39:1 letterbox, shallow depth. Grounded photoreal British social-realist crime-comedy texture; submerged. British spelling. No modern tech beyond 2011.
LIGHTING (Boys) — cold submerged booklight wrap-around, hard cold end: tight cool booklight close, crisp directional wrap, fast falloff into deep shadow — never a soft bath. Drowned cold-concrete / mint-tile base ~85%, one motivated source per frame (strip-lights / window contre-jour through steam), true negative fill. Accent: cold electric cyan + drowned teal in the murk.
COLOUR — 60:30:10 — cold mint-green tile (dominant) / steel-grey counter (secondary) / teal-cyan accent (hairnet, apron, chairs, strip-light murk).
═══ 3. LOCKS ═══
WB cold (submerged grade). Steam haze 15%. Axis along the counter; never cross.
⚡ ONE-LADLE RHYTHM (the spine): <<<9cfdf26f-ada4-42e1-b409-551631412bec>>> serves the moving queue — kid holds out a tray → ONE scoop of mash → kid moves on → next kid → ONE scoop → on. A brisk, living cadence; the line never stops.

⚡ KIDS LIVE BEHIND TERRANCE ONLY: moving <<<85a2a194-025c-42a9-81e6-d622687ccd09>>> only on the PUBLIC side; behind Horace is steamy kitchen (no kids).

STYLE
[LOOK] Live grime/rap gig at The Commons — a Victorian/industrial music hall (exposed brick, ornate plaster ceiling, iron upper balcony). Gritty, realistic, photographic. Heavy theatrical haze; a dominant GREEN/teal stage wash plus cool-white moving-head spotlight beams cutting the haze as solid volumetric shafts; dark, high-contrast, deep shadows, yet the performers' faces stay readable in the wash/spot. Warm practical accents far back: the amber-glowing bar, red EXIT signs, red wall sconces, and dozens of tiny bright phone screens in the crowd. Loud, packed, kinetic. Shot on a fast prime, slight grain, real handheld gig-doc energy.
[LIGHT + COLOR] One consistent stage-lighting model in every shot: a GREEN/teal wash is the dominant color; cool-white moving-head spot beams (hazy, volumetric) are the key/back light on the performers from the truss above and behind, so performers are rim/back-lit with the wash filling their faces; the crowd is lit by stage spill plus their own phone screens. Background practicals stay lit — amber bar, red EXIT, red sconces. High contrast, near-crushed blacks, but it always reads as a real gig (never pitch black). The wash breathes and the beams sweep with the beat. The lighting is ALIVE and pumps energy into the room: moving-head beams sweep, rotate and re-aim on the beat; hard white STROBE bursts — firing exactly like the reference <<<video_1>>>: full-frame pure-white single-frame flashes that blow the whole frame to white for an instant and snap straight back to black, in hard rhythmic bursts with no fade and no color — punch on the downbeats; the green wash pulses brighter and darker and occasionally shifts hue; rear blinders flare at the crowd now and then — the whole rig sweeps, pulses and flashes in time with the <<<audio_1>>>. CONTRE-JOUR — the stage is strongly BACKLIT: the performers on stage (the boys — Cal, Oli, Horace) are lit mainly from BEHIND and ABOVE by the truss beams and the bright hazy wash, so they read as shadowed, rim-lit figures / near-silhouettes — their faces and fronts mostly in shadow, catching only a faint green wash spill and the glow bouncing off the haze; the bright beams and smoke sit behind them. In closer shots just enough beam/wash grazes the near cheek and eyes for the emotion to still read, but the dominant look is contre-jour with the boys in shadow against the light.
[HAZE] [SMOKE IN EVERY SHOT — hard] EVERY single shot is full of thick theatrical smoke/haze, always visibly drifting and billowing in frame — it rolls across the stage, curls around the performers, hangs in and is sliced by the spot beams, and softens the deep background into glow. Fresh smoke is pumped in continuously (smoke-machine jets billow onto the stage), stirred by movement and air; the beams cut through it as solid shafts. Smoke fills the frame from the first frame to the last. Mounted above the stage, overhead smoke/hazer machines fire bursts of smoke straight DOWNWARD on the heavy beat drops and big punchline hits, so thick smoke cascades from above down over the performers (top-to-bottom), the white beams cutting through the falling smoke.
[CAMERA] Handheld, kinetic gig-doc energy — the camera is always moving and alive: it bobs and rides the beat, whip-pans between stage and crowd, pushes in on faces, swings around the performers; constant parallax between foreground, midground and the deep hazy hall. On hits/jolts the camera shakes hard. Keep ONE FOV per continuous shot (a FOV change reads as a cut). Direction stays consistent: the stage is one fixed side, the house/crowd the opposite. Per shot, state how the subject moves vs. how the background moves relative to the lens. Above all, the whole thing must FEEL like real, authentic live-concert footage — as if genuinely captured at the actual gig by real camera operators: down in the photo pit shooting up at the stage, out at front-of-house on long lenses punching through the crowd, and handheld among the people. Natural lens flares streak off the stage lights; the focus occasionally hunts and snaps back; framing is slightly imperfect and reactive, chasing the action a beat late; real crowd surges and stage energy. It should read as a genuine concert film / live broadcast / fan-shot gig, raw and alive.
[COVERAGE / SHOT SCALE] Cut this scene predominantly in CLOSE-UPS, MEDIUM shots and DETAIL/insert shots — tight, intimate, kinetic coverage of faces, eyes, hands, the mic, the phones, the decks, small gestures. Default to CU and MS, with detail inserts for objects and actions. WIDE / establishing shots are RARE; when one is used it is a TOP-DOWN AERIAL FLY-OVER — a drone/crane that swoops, glides and orbits high above the stage and crowd, looking down through the smoke and beams. STYLE
[LOOK] Live grime/rap gig at The Commons — a Victorian/industrial music hall (exposed brick, ornate plaster ceiling, iron upper balcony). Gritty, realistic, photographic. Heavy theatrical haze; a dominant GREEN/teal stage wash plus cool-white moving-head spotlight beams cutting the haze as solid volumetric shafts; dark, high-contrast, deep shadows, yet the performers' faces stay readable in the wash/spot. Warm practical accents far back: the amber-glowing bar, red EXIT signs, red wall sconces, and dozens of tiny bright phone screens in the crowd. Loud, packed, kinetic. Shot on a fast prime, slight grain, real handheld gig-doc energy.
[LIGHT + COLOR] One consistent stage-lighting model in every shot: a GREEN/teal wash is the dominant color; cool-white moving-head spot beams (hazy, volumetric) are the key/back light on the performers from the truss above and behind, so performers are rim/back-lit with the wash filling their faces; the crowd is lit by stage spill plus their own phone screens. Background practicals stay lit — amber bar, red EXIT, red sconces. High contrast, near-crushed blacks, but it always reads as a real gig (never pitch black). The wash breathes and the beams sweep with the beat. The lighting is ALIVE and pumps energy into the room: moving-head beams sweep, rotate and re-aim on the beat; hard white STROBE bursts — firing exactly like the reference <<<video_1>>>: full-frame pure-white single-frame flashes that blow the whole frame to white for an instant and snap straight back to black, in hard rhythmic bursts with no fade and no color — punch on the downbeats; the green wash pulses brighter and darker and occasionally shifts hue; rear blinders flare at the crowd now and then — the whole rig sweeps, pulses and flashes in time with the <<<audio_1>>>. CONTRE-JOUR — the stage is strongly BACKLIT: the performers on stage (the boys — Cal, Oli, Horace) are lit mainly from BEHIND and ABOVE by the truss beams and the bright hazy wash, so they read as shadowed, rim-lit figures / near-silhouettes — their faces and fronts mostly in shadow, catching only a faint green wash spill and the glow bouncing off the haze; the bright beams and smoke sit behind them. In closer shots just enough beam/wash grazes the near cheek and eyes for the emotion to still read, but the dominant look is contre-jour with the boys in shadow against the light.
[HAZE] [SMOKE IN EVERY SHOT — hard] EVERY single shot is full of thick theatrical smoke/haze, always visibly drifting and billowing in frame — it rolls across the stage, curls around the performers, hangs in and is sliced by the spot beams, and softens the deep background into glow. Fresh smoke is pumped in continuously (smoke-machine jets billow onto the stage), stirred by movement and air; the beams cut through it as solid shafts. Smoke fills the frame from the first frame to the last. Mounted above the stage, overhead smoke/hazer machines fire bursts of smoke straight DOWNWARD on the heavy beat drops and big punchline hits, so thick smoke cascades from above down over the performers (top-to-bottom), the white beams cutting through the falling smoke.
[CAMERA] Handheld, kinetic gig-doc energy — the camera is always moving and alive: it bobs and rides the beat, whip-pans between stage and crowd, pushes in on faces, swings around the performers; constant parallax between foreground, midground and the deep hazy hall. On hits/jolts the camera shakes hard. Keep ONE FOV per continuous shot (a FOV change reads as a cut). Direction stays consistent: the stage is one fixed side, the house/crowd the opposite. Per shot, state how the subject moves vs. how the background moves relative to the lens. Above all, the whole thing must FEEL like real, authentic live-concert footage — as if genuinely captured at the actual gig by real camera operators: down in the photo pit shooting up at the stage, out at front-of-house on long lenses punching through the crowd, and handheld among the people. Natural lens flares streak off the stage lights; the focus occasionally hunts and snaps back; framing is slightly imperfect and reactive, chasing the action a beat late; real crowd surges and stage energy. It should read as a genuine concert film / live broadcast / fan-shot gig, raw and alive.

WIDE / establishing shots are RARE; when one is used it is a TOP-DOWN AERIAL FLY-OVER — a drone/crane that swoops, glides and orbits high above the stage and crowd, looking down through the smoke and beams. Warm practical accents far back: the amber-glowing bar, red EXIT signs, red wall sconces, and dozens of tiny bright phone screens in the crowd. Loud, packed, kinetic. Background practicals stay lit — amber bar, red EXIT, red sconces. High contrast, near-crushed blacks, but it always reads as a real gig (never pitch black). The wash breathes and the beams sweep with the beat. 【动作·一镜到底·十秒编排（防随机）】①开头两拍＝人缝里的侧面构图：那撮不动的黑影、Nathan 在前、手下在后、全部石头侧脸盯着画框外的舞台方向；②台上一记重拍落下（词不在音轨里）——【周围炸了：旁边的小伙们指着他们大笑、一个笑得直不起腰、另一个凑近 Nathan 那侧咧着嘴吼笑（不碰他）】；③Nathan 三个微信号（喷气→咬肌一下→嘴角一撇）、平平地偏头："走了"——手下对视一眼、微点头；④【全组转身、肩膀顶着人流斜穿画面往吧台深处挤——背影被蹦跳的人浪一口一口吞掉、笑声和口哨追着、有人朝背影甩手起哄】——人浪合拢、手电海继续蹦。判废＝顺序乱/周围人不笑/任何 Ace 笑/走得从容体面或戏剧化（就是压着火的"行、走了"）。

The camera opens on a WIDE ESTABLISHING of the WHOLE ground-floor industrial garage (per <<<f94256f4-a96c-49ba-b4ed-4638b04a471e>>>), positioned DEEP inside — a long way BACK from the doors — so the whole workshop fills the frame and the wooden doors read SMALL in the far background. Scene 124-FINAL — THE LAST SHOT OF THE FILM. EXT. POLICE STATION — GREY OVERCAST DAY, the boiling location one last time: barriers, police, press, the fan sea, the chant. On the road before the station sits the marked POLICE CAR — and on its roof, tiny and impossible, sits the PINK HAWK-MOTH <<<169935ee-aa3f-4cc2-8976-b759d152becd>>> — the film's silent witness, present since the beginning. A car DOOR SLAMS shut below it — the jolt kicks the moth off the roof — and before leaving, it first DIPS LOW and THREADS ITS WAY THROUGH the roaring world it has watched all film: over the crowd, along the banner, around a lamp — and only then climbs a slow spiral into the white sky, the camera chasing it all the way, the car pulling away below — the film's full stop. TWO shots: a half-second wide, then one continuous ~14.5s final shot. ~15s TOTAL. Cinematic, poetic, grounded; everything in frame period-correct for 2011, British spelling.
THE SIZE LAW (hard rule, above all others): the moth is TINY and SLIGHT — its whole body is the size of a BABY'S LITTLE FINGER, and just as thin: a slender, narrow, tapered sliver of a body, a slip of a thing, all wings and almost no mass. It is smaller than any thumb in the crowd, smaller than every hand and fist it passes; a stick-board is fifty times its size; on the car roof it is a speck beside the lightbar; against the sky it is a dot. The reference controls its COLOURS and ANATOMY ONLY — NEVER its scale or bulk. The only frames where it reads large are the true MACRO frames, where the lens is centimetres away. If the moth's wing pattern is readable from a wide or a crowd-distance frame, or its body reads plump and heavy, the moth is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FLIGHT LAW (hard rule): the moth flies CHAOTICALLY, like a butterfly — never a straight line, never a smooth arc: a constant fluttering JINK — up, down, left, right — small sharp random deviations stitched through every metre of its route; it bobs, drops a hand-span, flicks sideways, rises, staggers on the air, catches itself, flutters on. The ROUTE (roof → low drop → crowd → banner → lamp → spiral → sky) is where it's going; the chaotic flutter is HOW it goes there, every second of the way, in real time.
THE CHASE LAW (hard rule — the camera): the camera behaves like a live operator TRYING to keep the fluttering moth CENTRED — and always a breath behind: every jink pulls the moth off-centre and the frame CORRECTS after it — small human catch-up pans and tilts, tiny overshoots, re-centres — the moth dancing around the middle of the frame, never nailed to it. The big move (dive, low track, corkscrew, helix, hold) stays smooth and continuous underneath; the fine chasing corrections live on top of it. The moth leads; the camera follows.

🎨 STYLE PREFIX
STYLE PREFIX — WORLD OF DMITRY (Variant A · Balabanov × Scorsese)
OPTICS
Long-lens compressed observation for the watcher — 8° super-telephoto (flattened background wash, foreground occlusion), 18° classic telephoto to isolate a target across distance. 47° standard normal, flat and deadpan, for plain interiors and open country; through-glass and long-lens observation framing. One lens locked per shot.
CAMERA
Balabanov base register: static observational framing, locked off on sticks or a long lens through glass, the subject often small and matter-of-fact in a wide plain frame, no reframing while watching — patient stillness and dead air. Scorsese kinetics on the strike: a single motivated push-in as the predator locks on, a surveillance-to-strike snap of energy, a hard focus snap onto the target, the occasional freeze-frame beat, a whip-pan on sudden movement, energy cut to sound. Every move motivated — cold, exact competence; the camera as patient and indifferent as the man.
LIGHTING
Shaped by a booklight wrap-around kept at the coldest, flattest end of the scale — a cool booklight with little diffusion, even and observational, minimal wrap, no warmth in the bounce. Cold flat naturalistic field ~85% — wet-asphalt and steel greys, fog and breath-vapour. Motivated accents only and always cold or harsh: cold artificial sources, headlight beams and dash glow, sodium haze in fog, a brief cold flash, a cold moon over open country. Dawn comes as a thin cold grey-gold, never warm or romantic.
STYLE
Photoreal cold post-Soviet realism — deadpan, mundane menace, dry melancholy, lived-in surfaces, violence delivered plainly and without glamour. Flat realism over kinetic punch — indifferent, exact, lethal.

FORMAT / OPTICS / CAMERA

ACTION
0.0–1.5s — THE AIM: Cal in profile, ball raised to his set point, knees loaded, eyes easy on his line off screen-left — COOL and unbothered, almost casual, but every part of him gathered: a slow exhale, a tiny settle of the shoulders, the calm of someone who's made this shot a thousand times. Around him the crowd is already HYPING — bouncing lightly on their toes, hands half-raised ready to throw up, faces split with anticipation, mouths going, everyone locked on Cal waiting for the make.
1.5–2.3s — THE SHOT: smooth, effortless power — legs drive, elbow to full extension, the wrist whips through — the ball rips off his fingertips and is gone out of frame-left; the follow-through hangs easy, his face still calm, watching his line.
2.3–4.0s — THE MAKE: a held beat — the crowd frozen mid-bounce — then it DROPS off-screen and everything ERUPTS: arms flying up, heads thrown back, bodies jumping — and Cal breaks too, the cool cracking into a huge grin, fist pumped, turning into the crowd as a hand slams his shoulder and someone grabs him round the neck — celebrating WITH them, lit up. HOLD in the eruption. END.
We NEVER see where the ball goes — no hoop, no arc landing; only Cal.
Exactly ONE Cal in the shot — no lookalikes in the crowd.

The ball real: true weight at the set point, backspin ripping off the fingers, gone on a natural arc out of frame-left. The shot mechanics fluid and grounded — load, drive, release in one easy chain. Night mist drifting; breath faintly visible. Clean hands and faces everywhere.

AUDIO

STYLE
Photoreal British social-realist crime film, London 2011, shot like a grime video: one boy shooting like it's nothing while the whole estate holds its breath — then everybody loses it together. Nothing modern beyond 2011. British spelling.

Somewhere out of frame a car door thumps shut — the car ROCKS once on its springs — and the shake lifts the moth off the lightbar; before leaving, it first DIPS LOW and FLUTTERS ITS WAY THROUGH the roaring world it has watched all film: over the crowd, along the banner, around a lamp — the camera FLYING with it the whole way like a smooth FPV drone — and then it climbs, the camera rising with it and LEVELLING OUT into one final, beautiful, held COMPOSITION: the AERIAL VIEW of LONDON per <<<bd0faecb-2efa-4ece-9e32-51a7b6800ded>>> — and across that settled frame the moth flutters on, dwindles, and is lost into the city haze — the film's full stop. TWO shots: a half-second wide, then one continuous ~14.5s final shot. ~15s TOTAL. Cinematic, poetic, grounded; everything in frame period-correct for 2011, British spelling.
THE SIZE LAW (hard rule, above all others): the moth is TINY and SLIGHT — the whole moth, wings and all, is NO BIGGER THAN A COIN; its body is a thin sliver, skinnier than a matchstick — narrow, tapered, a slip of a thing, all wings and almost no mass. It is smaller than any thumb in the crowd, smaller than every hand and fist it passes; a stick-board is a hundred times its size; on the lightbar it is a speck; against the London aerial it is a dot. The reference controls its COLOURS and ANATOMY ONLY — NEVER its scale or bulk. The only frames where it reads large are the true MACRO frames, where the lens is centimetres away. If the moth's wing pattern is readable from a wide or a crowd-distance frame, or its body reads plump and heavy, the moth is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FLIGHT LAW (hard rule — TRUE BUTTERFLY FLIGHT): the wings NEVER stop beating — a constant rapid four-wing flicker from the first frame of flight to the last; the moth stays airborne on wingbeats alone, its featherweight body BOUNCING lightly with them: each burst of beats lifts it a few centimetres, it sinks a touch between bursts — a lively, dancing, slightly irregular flutter, rising and dipping and wavering side to side in small continuous amounts as it travels — airy, weightless, quick, always moving, always a little unsteady, the way a real butterfly crosses a garden. The path stays READABLE — one continuous meandering line, its wobbles small and constant rather than violent — and every metre of it is flown, beat by beat, in real time. If the moth holds its wings open and SAILS like a little bird, the flight is wrong and the shot is wrong.
THE MOTH-INTEGRATION LAW (hard rule — LIGHT & COLOUR, so it never looks comped or cartoonish): the moth is lit ONLY by the scene's own flat cold overcast daylight — it has NO key of its own, no glow, no invented rim-light, no bright sheen the sky wouldn't give it. Its pinks and olives read MUTED, cool and MATTE under the grey top-light — softly desaturated exactly as real wing-scales look under an overcast sky, never vivid, never candy-bright, never backlit-glowing, never a crisp sticker laid over the plate. It sits in the SAME grade, contrast, black level and colour temperature as everything around it — the same soft shadowless top-light, the same wet-cool ambient bounce off the tarmac — and it CATCHES its environment: a faint cool sheen of white sky along the wing-tops, the crowd's colour as the faintest ambient tint from below, the blue police lamp's cold spill brushing one flank for only half a second on the turn. It throws its own TINY soft contact shadow and stirs a tiny reflection wherever it passes close to a surface. Its EDGES are soft and photographic, sitting inside the lens's shallow focus with real fall-off — never cut-out-sharp against the background — and it carries the SAME grain and the SAME natural motion blur as the plate. If the moth ever looks brighter, more saturated, sharper-edged, harder-lit or "stuck on" compared to the world it flies through, it is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FPV LAW (hard rule — the camera): the camera is a SMOOTH FPV DRONE — it FLIES, it never cranes: one continuous piloted flight with real momentum, living in the air beside the moth — it SWOOPS down off the car with it, SKIMS low over the tarmac, CARVES banking arcs over the crowd, BANKS gently into the lamp turn with a few degrees of natural roll, SOARS up the climb and eases out level at the top — every manoeuvre leaning into the moth's route the way a pilot flies a line. But a CALM pilot: wide rounded arcs, gradual accelerations and decelerations, soft gentle rolls, every turn eased in and eased out — flowing, carving, alive — with zero snap: the energy lives in the continuous forward flow, never in jerks. It keeps the bouncing moth NEAR the centre, letting the flutter dance a little inside the frame. The flight ENDS in stillness: on the last beat the drone levels into the final London composition, bleeds off its speed and SETTLES to a hover-stop — and from that settled frame, the MOTH does the leaving while the camera stays put. The moth is lively; the drone is fluid; that partnership is the shot.

THE SIZE LAW (hard rule, above all others): the moth is TINY and SLIGHT — the whole moth, wings and all, is NO BIGGER THAN A COIN; its body is a thin sliver, skinnier than a matchstick — narrow, tapered, a slip of a thing, all wings and almost no mass. It is smaller than any thumb in the crowd, smaller than every hand and fist it passes; a stick-board is a hundred times its size; on the lightbar it is a speck; against the London aerial it is a dot. The reference controls its COLOURS and ANATOMY ONLY — NEVER its scale or bulk. The only frames where it reads large are the true MACRO frames, where the lens is centimetres away — the opening perch and the instant it sweeps PAST the lens on its exit. If the moth's wing pattern is readable from a wide or a crowd-distance frame, or its body reads plump and heavy, the moth is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FLIGHT LAW (hard rule — TRUE BUTTERFLY FLIGHT): the wings NEVER stop beating — a constant rapid four-wing flicker from the first frame of flight to the last; the moth stays airborne on wingbeats alone, its featherweight body BOUNCING lightly with them: each burst of beats lifts it a few centimetres, it sinks a touch between bursts — a lively, dancing, slightly irregular flutter, rising and dipping and wavering side to side in small continuous amounts as it travels — airy, weightless, quick, always moving, always a little unsteady, the way a real butterfly crosses a garden. The path stays READABLE — one continuous meandering line, its wobbles small and constant rather than violent — and every metre of it is flown, beat by beat, in real time. The one burst of real SPEED is the final dart past the lens — still driven by hard wingbeats, a committed hawk-moth sprint, never a sailing glide. If the moth holds its wings open and SAILS like a little bird, the flight is wrong and the shot is wrong.
THE MOTH-INTEGRATION LAW (hard rule — LIGHT & COLOUR, so it never looks comped or cartoonish): the moth is lit ONLY by the scene's own flat cold overcast daylight — it has NO key of its own, no glow, no invented rim-light, no bright sheen the sky wouldn't give it. Its pinks and olives read MUTED, cool and MATTE under the grey top-light — softly desaturated exactly as real wing-scales look under an overcast sky, never vivid, never candy-bright, never backlit-glowing, never a crisp sticker laid over the plate. It sits in the SAME grade, contrast, black level and colour temperature as everything around it — the same soft shadowless top-light, the same wet-cool ambient bounce off the tarmac — and it CATCHES its environment: a faint cool sheen of white sky along the wing-tops, the crowd's colour as the faintest ambient tint from below, the blue police lamp's cold spill brushing one flank for only half a second on the turn. It throws its own TINY soft contact shadow and stirs a tiny reflection wherever it passes close to a surface. Its EDGES are soft and photographic, sitting inside the lens's shallow focus with real fall-off — never cut-out-sharp against the background — and it carries the SAME grain and the SAME natural motion blur as the plate (heaviest on the fast exit past the lens). If the moth ever looks brighter, more saturated, sharper-edged, harder-lit or "stuck on" compared to the world it flies through, it is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FPV LAW (hard rule — the camera): the camera is a SMOOTH FPV DRONE — it FLIES, it never cranes: one continuous piloted flight with real momentum, living in the air beside the moth — it SWOOPS down off the car with it, SKIMS low over the tarmac, CARVES banking arcs over the crowd, BANKS gently into the lamp turn with a few degrees of natural roll, SOARS up the climb and eases out level at the top — every manoeuvre leaning into the moth's route the way a pilot flies a line. But a CALM pilot: wide rounded arcs, gradual accelerations and decelerations, soft gentle rolls, every turn eased in and eased out — flowing, carving, alive — with zero snap: the energy lives in the continuous forward flow, never in jerks. It keeps the bouncing moth NEAR the centre, letting the flutter dance a little inside the frame. The flight ENDS in stillness: on the last beat the drone levels into the final London composition, bleeds off its speed and SETTLES to a hover-stop, and then the camera HOLDS DEAD STILL — and from that settled frame the MOTH does the leaving: it turns and flies FAST back toward the lens and SWEEPS PAST THE CAMERA, close and quick, out of frame past the camera, while the drone never moves. The moth is lively; the drone is fluid, then still; that partnership is the shot.

THE SIZE LAW (hard rule, above all others): the moth is TINY and SLIGHT — the whole moth, wings and all, is NO BIGGER THAN A COIN; its body is a thin sliver, skinnier than a matchstick — narrow, tapered, a slip of a thing, all wings and almost no mass. It is smaller than any thumb in the crowd, smaller than every hand and fist it passes; a stick-board is a hundred times its size; on the lightbar it is a speck; against the London aerial it is a dot. The reference controls its COLOURS and ANATOMY ONLY — NEVER its scale or bulk. The only frames where it reads large are the true MACRO frames, where the lens is centimetres away — the opening perch and the instant it sweeps PAST the lens on its exit. If the moth's wing pattern is readable from a wide or a crowd-distance frame, or its body reads plump and heavy, the moth is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FLIGHT LAW (hard rule — TRUE BUTTERFLY FLIGHT): the wings NEVER stop beating — a constant rapid four-wing flicker from the first frame of flight to the last; the moth stays airborne on wingbeats alone, its featherweight body BOUNCING lightly with them: each burst of beats lifts it a few centimetres, it sinks a touch between bursts — a lively, dancing, slightly irregular flutter, rising and dipping and wavering side to side in small continuous amounts as it travels — airy, weightless, quick, always moving, always a little unsteady, the way a real butterfly crosses a garden. The path stays READABLE — one continuous meandering line, its wobbles small and constant rather than violent — and every metre of it is flown, beat by beat, in real time. The one burst of real SPEED is the final dart past the lens — still driven by hard wingbeats, a committed hawk-moth sprint, never a sailing glide. If the moth holds its wings open and SAILS like a little bird, the flight is wrong and the shot is wrong.
THE MOTH-INTEGRATION LAW (hard rule — LIGHT & COLOUR, so it never looks comped or cartoonish): the moth is lit ONLY by the scene's own flat cold overcast daylight — it has NO key of its own, no glow, no invented rim-light, no bright sheen the sky wouldn't give it. Its pinks and olives read MUTED, cool and MATTE under the grey top-light — softly desaturated exactly as real wing-scales look under an overcast sky, never vivid, never candy-bright, never backlit-glowing, never a crisp sticker laid over the plate. It sits in the SAME grade, contrast, black level and colour temperature as everything around it — the same soft shadowless top-light, the same wet-cool ambient bounce off the tarmac — and it CATCHES its environment: a faint cool sheen of white sky along the wing-tops, the crowd's colour as the faintest ambient tint from below, the blue police lamp's cold spill brushing one flank for only half a second on the turn. It throws its own TINY soft contact shadow and stirs a tiny reflection wherever it passes close to a surface. Its EDGES are soft and photographic, sitting inside the lens's shallow focus with real fall-off — never cut-out-sharp against the background — and it carries the SAME grain and the SAME natural motion blur as the plate (heaviest on the fast exit past the lens). If the moth ever looks brighter, more saturated, sharper-edged, harder-lit or "stuck on" compared to the world it flies through, it is WRONG and the shot is wrong.
THE FPV LAW (hard rule — the camera, a HERO one-take with signature moves): the camera is a SMOOTH FPV DRONE — it FLIES, it never cranes: one continuous piloted flight with real momentum, living in the air beside the moth, choreographed as a show-off one-take that still stays CARVED, never snapped. Its repertoire, layered through the shot: (a) a slow ORBITAL PUSH-IN creeping around the perched moth to open; (b) a reactive DROP-AND-SWOOP off the car with a touch of following roll; (c) a low GROUND-SKIM inches off the wet tarmac, the moth's reflection streaking; (d) a FOREGROUND REVEAL — sliding out from behind the red PHONE BOX / the Union Jack edge so the object wipes the lens and unveils the crowd canyon; (e) a THREAD flying the gap between two raised boards like a gate; (f) an OVERTAKE — the drone slips BEHIND the moth, then surges AHEAD and swings to face it, flying backwards to LEAD the moth head-on for a beat; (g) banking S-weaves with RACK-FOCUS handoffs between near heads and the moth; (h) a rising TRUCK along the banner; (i) a mid-air ORBIT circling the HOVERING moth at the pole-top, swinging 180°+ so the whole crowd wheels behind the still insect; (j) a full CORKSCREW SPIRAL around the lamp opening into a GOD'S-EYE TOP-DOWN, which then TILTS UP to bring the London skyline/horizon into frame; (k) an ascending CORKSCREW climb, the city wheeling below; (l) foreground WIPES (board, pole, phone-box) sweeping close across the lens as natural transitions; (m) a gentle DUTCH tilt in the energy that RESOLVES to dead-level for the final aerial. Every one of these is eased IN and eased OUT — wide rounded arcs, gradual accelerations and decelerations, soft gentle rolls, zero whip, zero jerk; the energy lives in continuous flow and in the LAYERING of these moves, not in snaps. It keeps the bouncing moth NEAR frame centre, letting the flutter dance a little inside the frame. The flight ENDS in stillness: the drone levels into the final London composition, bleeds off its speed and SETTLES to a hover-stop, and then the camera HOLDS DEAD STILL — and from that settled frame the MOTH does the leaving: it turns and flies FAST back toward the lens and SWEEPS PAST THE CAMERA, close and quick, out of frame past the camera, while the drone never moves. The moth is lively; the drone is fluid and inventive, then still; that partnership is the shot.

Style: 8K IMAX, photorealistic late-autumn South-East London crime-comedy. Real 35mm film grain and halation. NOT 3D render, NOT game engine, NOT game-cutscene aesthetic, NOT cartoon.

Physics: gravity and inertia respected — real mass and weight, correct contact shadows, no floating props.
Composition: rule of thirds + golden ratio; motivated motion from frame one; staged depth (foreground / mid / background).
Continuity: characters, props and environment identical across every cut — no identity drift. Recurring motifs (the pink-and-olive Elephant Hawk-moth; the glossy clean RED lifeboat) are the only elements that cross between worlds.
Technical: 24fps smooth motion, 8K detail, no jitter, no flicker, no slow-motion unless specified.

PHYSICS
Real weight transfer throughout, careful muted tiptoe steps, heel kept off the ground, knees soft. The door closes with hinge weight and a soft latch, no slam. The notice tears with a paper rip and crumples with crisp foil-like creasing. Cold breath-vapour leaves both mouths in the foggy air. Wet concrete throws soft cold reflections; Cal's track jacket and Maggie's heavy robe move with a half-beat cloth delay; her hoop earrings sway with her head. Distant laundry stirs faintly; bin bags sag with weight.

LIGHTING
Cold and submerged exterior morning, graded at the hard cold end. Flat foggy daylight is the cold key — drowned khaki, wet-asphalt and cold-concrete base field, true negative fill, never flat front light. The accent is a cold current of electric cyan and drowned teal pooling in the wet floor and in the depth of the fog. The one warm motivated note in segment 1 is a faint sodium-amber glow at the door seam, falling off fast; the stairwell corner in segment 2 carries a cold flat light with deeper shadow in the well. Expose for the bright foggy skyline beyond the parapet, not for the faces; faces and walkway sit cool and low, eyes and wet speculars catching the cold light.

AUDIO
No music. Cold estate ambience — distant traffic, wind, dripping water, a far-off dog.
Cal speaks one quiet line, low and defeated, under his breath at 2.4s–3.2s as he reads the notice: "ahh fuck". His voice, paste verbatim — "A 25-year-old English man. Smooth, relaxed mid-range baritone; casual, unscripted, and conversational delivery; nostalgic and warmly reflective, sharing a personal memory with a natural, steady pace." Ambience ducks under his line; close, clean, intimate.
From 4.0s, down the walkway, a MAN and a WOMAN argue at the neighbour's open door — Maggie is the woman; the man is unseen inside. Their overlapping argument stays muffled and ducked low behind Cal; no clean scripted line for them, no front-facing lip-sync for Maggie since she is turned into the doorway. Otherwise Cal is silent — soft breaths, the latch, paper tearing and careful steps carry the cut. No narration, no subtitles.

STYLE
Grounded photoreal British social-realist crime-comedy texture. Desaturated cool grade, blacks lifted into green-cyan, cyan and teal pushed in the cool range, no warm note in the field except the faint sodium door-seam glow. Heavy, pressed-down, submerged estate mood.

QUALITY
Sharp clarity, stable picture, vintage spherical character with subtle anamorphic, no grain, no overexposure, no blur, no ghosting, no modern tech beyond 2011. British spelling.

@c01de842-… 背对仍敞开的后备厢，站定原地，扫视庭院——搜寻他感觉到的某个人。就在此刻一小块石头砸中他的头：一块儿童拳头大小的混凝土碎块（无插销标记——由 Seedance 渲染）从上方落下，擦过他头后部一记斜掠的撞击，然后弹开，落在他旁边的沥青上。后备厢保持敞开。

@713b137a-…。Dmitri 在 @fda50348-… 车尾，敞开的后备厢在他身后；棕砖、封死的蓝绿车库门、带粉色涂鸦的立柱、湿沥青。平视——高处不取过道；石头从顶边进入，来源不可见。
首帧与空间调度

Dmitri 居中（x≈50%，y≈48%），转身面向院子，敞开的后备厢在他身后虚化（x≈58%，y≈55%）；他的头略微低垂，使头后部朝上。

单一连续镜头，约 5 秒，实时。

63° 对角视场（35mm 观感）；机位约 3 米，平视，略带 3/4 角度。

锁定／极细微现场稳定晃动；石头撞击时一记小猛震；不游移，不仰拍。
动作时序

0.0–1.5 Dmitri 背对敞开的后备厢，扫视院子。1.5–3.5 眯眼搜寻——他确信有人在那里，朝外凝视，紧张。3.5–4.2 一块儿童拳头大小的石头从顶边落入，擦掠他头后部一记斜掠的撞击（无预备动作，来源不可见）。4.2–5.0 石头弹开、哐啷落到他旁边的沥青上；Dmitri 一震，发懵，开始要垮下去。

平板灰色阴天，柔和；提亮的灰绿暗部；沥青上的潮湿光泽。
声音

住宅区环境声——毛毛雨、远处车流、风；一口紧张的屏息，然后一记沉闷的斜掠咔嚓和石头在沥青上滑动的声音。无对白，无音乐。
质量

锐利、稳定，脸与斜掠撞击可读；无重影，无闪烁。
正向约束

Dmitri 背对仍敞开的后备厢，在院子里搜寻某人；一块儿童拳头大小的石头（无插销标记，来源不可见）斜掠过他头后部并落在他旁边；后备厢保持敞开；画面中只有 Dmitri；平视——无儿童，高处不取天桥。

单一连续镜头，约 6 秒，实时。

低位锁定在地面；他落地时极轻微现场稳定晃动；停在伤口上。不游移。

锐利可读的伤口与缓慢的血；倒落时自然的运动模糊；节奏稳定；无重影，无闪烁。
